docs.title: ADR-0001: Monorepo with earned abstractions
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-07-31

docs.title: Context
docs.text: This lab consists of four planned systems (Macro Research Digest, Filings Intelligence, Deal & Comps Platform, Research Agent), built by a solo developer over roughly six to twelve months, alongside full-time study and elite athletic training. Available development time is limited to a few hours per week. The systems are related — they will eventually share data access patterns, LLM calling conventions, and validation logic — but only one system exists at the start.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Use a single repository (ai-finance-lab) containing all systems, rather than a separate repository per system or a GitHub organisation. Within it, apps/ holds one directory per system, and core/ holds shared modules.

core/ starts empty. A module is extracted into it only once three separate applications independently need the same functionality — not before. Until the third real need appears, duplication between apps is accepted as the correct state, not a defect to be pre-emptively solved.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Easier: one CI pipeline, one dependency lockfile, one documentation site, one commit history that reads as a coherent build log rather than four disconnected efforts. A reviewer sees one system, not four half efforts. Refactoring across systems (when it eventually happens) is a single-repo operation, not a cross-repo coordination problem.

Harder: early on, some code will be duplicated between apps/macro_note and whatever the second system turns out to be, before core/ exists to hold it. This is accepted deliberately — it is cheaper to tolerate duplication for a few months than to guess at the wrong abstraction now and have to unwind it later, which is the more common and more expensive failure mode for a solo, time-constrained developer.

Risk accepted knowingly: if the systems turn out to be far less similar than expected, the monorepo structure and the rule-of-three discipline will have cost little, since core/ was never populated on spec in the first place.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Multi-repo (one repository per system). Rejected. For a solo developer, this means four separate CI configurations to maintain, four separate dependency lockfiles that can drift out of sync with each other, and a portfolio that reads to a reviewer as four thin, disconnected projects rather than one coherent system. The coordination overhead of keeping four repositories consistent is not justified until there is a team, or until a system genuinely needs independent deployment.

GitHub organisation with one repo per system. Rejected for the same reasons as multi-repo, with the added overhead of managing an organisation for a single-person project. Revisit only if a system needs to be deployed, licensed, or open-sourced independently of the others.

Shared core/ library populated upfront, before any application exists. Rejected. Designing shared abstractions before a second (let alone third) concrete use case exists means guessing at the right shape of the abstraction. Abstractions designed this way are reliably wrong, because the actual requirements are not yet known. The rule of three exists specifically to prevent this failure mode.

docs.title: ADR-0002: DuckDB over Postgres
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-08-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md named DuckDB over Parquet files as the analytics store from the start of the project, but deferred the reasoning to the point where a real persistence requirement existed to reason about. That point is now: the Macro Research Digest has three working connectors (FRED, RBA, a yfinance wrapper) that each produce Observations on their own schedule, with genuinely different failure shapes (FRED and RBA fail loud with a typed exception; the market connector never raises and signals "unavailable" as an empty list). All three need a common place to land so that a fetch can be re-run without duplicating data, and so a future orchestration layer can ask "what's the last known value for this series" when a source fails.

The operating context has not changed since ADR-0001: one developer, part-time hours, a GitHub Actions cron as the only scheduler, and — the concrete fact that matters most for this decision — exactly one writer. The daily digest run is a single sequential process; nothing else writes to this store concurrently, and nothing ever will under the current architecture. There is no application server, no request-handling process that would need a second connection into the same database while the cron job runs.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Persist Observations in a single DuckDB database file (data/macro_note.duckdb) containing one table, keyed on (series_id, obs_date, source). Idempotent upsert is DuckDB's native INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE, not hand-rolled merge logic.

Every write also re-exports the full table to data/observations.parquet via DuckDB's COPY ... TO ... (FORMAT PARQUET). That Parquet file is the "Parquet files on local disk" half of the original architecture line: a portable, DuckDB-independent copy that any other tool — a notebooks/ exploration, a future app in this same repo, or just duckdb from a terminal — can read directly, without this codebase or a running instance of ObservationStore involved at all. The application itself never reads the Parquet file back; it is one-way output, not a second source of truth.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Easier: upsert, the single hardest part of "never create duplicates on re-run," is a single SQL statement with a PRIMARY KEY doing the enforcement, rather than application code reading, deduplicating, and rewriting files by hand. latest() and history() are plain indexed SQL queries. There is no server process to start, configure, monitor, or keep patched — ObservationStore opens a file and closes it, which is the entire operational surface. Backing up or inspecting the data is copying one .duckdb file and one .parquet file; either can be opened cold, with no schema migration tool and no running service, by anyone with a Python shell.

Harder: DuckDB's file format allows exactly one writer at a time. If a second application in this monorepo ever needs to write to the same store concurrently — not read, write — this design stops working and something with real concurrent-write support would be needed. That is treated as acceptable, not overlooked: nothing in the current or near-term roadmap introduces a second writer, and per the rule of three, building for concurrent writes before a second writer exists would be the exact mistake ADR-0001 already argued against.

Risk accepted knowingly: a single .duckdb file is a single point of failure with no replication. For a personal research tool re-derivable from public data sources (FRED, RBA, Yahoo Finance all retain history), losing the file costs a backfill, not a business, so this is judged an acceptable risk rather than one requiring redundancy.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Postgres. Rejected. Postgres is a server: a process to run, a port to open, a version to patch, credentials to manage. None of that buys anything here — there is no concurrent access to serve and no other consumer that needs to reach the data over a network. Running a database server to serve a single-writer, single-reader daily batch job is the exact kind of infrastructure CLAUDE.md rules out on principle (§8: no Postgres, no Docker), not just on cost.

SQLite. A closer call than Postgres, and a real contender: also a single embedded file, also zero-operations. Rejected specifically because this data is analytical, not transactional — the queries this store exists to serve (latest(), history() over a lookback window, and future period-over-period calculations) are columnar scans and aggregations over a time series, which is DuckDB's design center. SQLite is optimized for row-oriented reads and writes of individual records, not for this shape of query, and has no native Parquet support — reading or writing Parquet from SQLite would mean adding a separate library, whereas DuckDB does both natively in the same engine already chosen for querying.

Parquet files with no database at all. Rejected. This was seriously considered, since Parquet alone would satisfy "local disk, no server." The problem is upsert: Parquet files have no row-level update or a native uniqueness constraint, so idempotent re-runs would require reading the existing file, deduplicating in application code, and rewriting the whole file on every single fetch — reinventing, by hand, exactly what a PRIMARY KEY and ON CONFLICT already do for free. DuckDB gives that guarantee natively while still producing a Parquet file as output, so there was no real tradeoff being given up by keeping DuckDB in the loop.

These are not part of the Systems above, and they are not governed by the numeric fidelity invariant described in LLM Usage Standards.

That invariant — language models never produce numbers, every figure is computed in Python and validated before publication — applies to the automated pipelines: Macro Research Digest, Filings Intelligence, Deal & Comps Platform, and Research Agent. It does not apply here.

Figures in this section were researched and compiled by hand, from public disclosures and press coverage, working in Excel. AI assistance was used for drafting prose and search, the same way it might assist any analyst, but the numbers themselves were not computed or guard-checked by a Python pipeline. Treat this section as a portfolio of applied financial analysis work, not as output from the engineered systems.

docs.text:
Prepared by Tyler Krenkels — self-directed case study, not affiliated with any party to the transaction. See Case Studies for how figures in this write-up were sourced and why it sits outside the numeric fidelity invariant that governs the Systems.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Insignia Financial Ltd, Australia's largest listed diversified wealth management group with roughly $340 billion in funds under management and administration (FUMA), was acquired by CC Capital Partners in a scheme of arrangement that completed in April 2026, ending a 16-month competitive process that at various points involved three private equity bidders: CC Capital, Bain Capital and Brookfield Asset Management.

The final scheme price of $4.80 per share implied an equity value of approximately $3.3 billion and a 57% premium to the undisturbed share price of $3.06 on 11 December 2024. Notably, the final price came in below the ~$5.00 per share peak reached during the competitive phase of the process in March 2025, after both Bain Capital and Brookfield withdrew. This case study reconstructs the process, values each stage of the bidding using a consistent EV/EBITDA framework, and sets out the judgment calls a Financial Sponsors or M&A advisory team would have had to make at each stage.

docs.title: 1. Company Overview
docs.text:
Insignia Financial (formerly IOOF, and prior to that incorporating the MLC business acquired from National Australia Bank in 2021) operated across four lines of business: Master Trust (superannuation), Wrap platforms, Advice (including the Shadforth network), and Asset Management (including multi-asset and fixed income capabilities). The FY25 result marked a turning point operationally: statutory NPAT returned to positive territory at $16.1 million after a $185.3 million loss in FY24, driven by the completion of the MLC-NAB separation, resolution of legacy advice remediation costs, and delivery of cost optimisation targets.

Metric FY23 FY24 FY25 TTM (Dec-25) Revenue ($m) 1,948 1,942 1,581 1,642 EBITDA ($m) 289.7 130.1 393.3 412.7 EBITDA Margin 14.9% 6.7% 24.9% 25.1% Statutory NPAT ($m) 51.4 (185.3) 16.1 111.7 FUMA ($bn, period-end/avg) n/a 319.6 323.0 (avg) 342.0

The FY24 EBITDA trough reflects roughly $237 million of unusual items, principally advice remediation, legal settlements and transformation costs tied to the NAB separation, which is why FY25's clean result was central to how bidders underwrote forward earnings.

docs.title: 2. Deal Timeline and the Shape of the Contest
docs.text:
The process ran through three distinct phases: an initial approach and price discovery period, a competitive three-way phase with exclusivity granted to two bidders simultaneously, and a final consolidation phase once two of the three bidders withdrew.

Phase 1 — Initial Approach (Dec 2024 – Jan 2025)

  • Bain Capital made an initial non-binding indicative proposal in December 2024, using the 11 December 2024 closing price of $3.06 as the last undisturbed reference point.
  • CC Capital and Bain Capital both revised proposals to $4.60 per share by late January 2025.

Phase 2 — Three-Way Competitive Process (Feb – May 2025)

  • Brookfield Capital Partners (UK) entered the process in February 2025, matching the $4.60 offer and securing limited due diligence access — turning a two-horse race into a genuine three-way contest.
  • By March 2025, Bain Capital and CC Capital had both sweetened their bids to $5.00 per share, and Insignia's board signed exclusivity deeds with both simultaneously, an unusual structure that kept optionality alive while narrowing the field.
  • The exclusivity period was extended to allow both remaining bidders to arrange debt financing and complete due diligence.

Phase 3 — Consolidation and Binding Offer (May 2025 – Apr 2026)

  • Bain Capital withdrew in May 2025, citing macro uncertainty in global markets as the reason it could not proceed to a binding proposal — a reminder that even at exclusivity stage, financing and macro conditions can still kill a deal.
  • Brookfield did not match the improved terms and dropped out of contention around the same time, leaving CC Capital as the sole remaining bidder.
  • Insignia entered a binding Scheme Implementation Deed with CC Capital (via Daintree BidCo) on 22 July 2025, at $4.80 per share — below the $5.00 peak reached during active competition.
  • An independent expert deemed the offer fair and reasonable in February 2026; shareholders voted to approve in April 2026 with support in the high-80s to high-90s percentage range; the Federal Court approved the scheme on 16 April 2026; and the transaction completed on 28 April 2026, with Insignia delisted from the ASX on 29 April 2026.

docs.title: 3. Valuation Across the Bidding Process
docs.text:
Applying a consistent EV/EBITDA framework across each stage of the process (full detail and formulas in the accompanying Excel model) shows how the implied multiple moved as the contest evolved:

Stage Price/Share Equity Value EV EV/FY25 EBITDA Premium to Undisturbed Undisturbed (11-Dec-24) $3.06 $2,044m $2,477m 6.3x - Initial matched bids (Jan 2025) $4.60 $3,073m $3,505m 8.9x 50.3% Peak competitive bid (Mar 2025) $5.00 $3,340m $3,773m 9.6x 63.4% Final Scheme price (Jul 2025) $4.80 $3,206m $3,639m 9.3x 56.9%

The 56.9% premium implied by this framework closely matches Insignia's own disclosed 57% premium figure, which is a useful sense-check on the net debt and share count assumptions used (set out in the model's Valuation Analysis tab). The more interesting story is the ~4% price decline from the $5.00 peak to the $4.80 final price: once the field narrowed from three bidders to one, CC Capital had materially less competitive tension to price against, and the final terms reflect that shift in bargaining power as much as any change in Insignia's underlying fundamentals.

docs.title: 4. Key Judgment Calls (Advisory Perspective)
docs.text:
If advising Insignia's board through this process, several decision points stand out as genuinely difficult calls rather than obvious ones:

  • Running dual exclusivity in March 2025 (signing exclusivity deeds with both Bain and CC Capital simultaneously) kept competitive tension alive for longer than a single-bidder exclusivity period would have, which likely contributed to the $4.60 → $5.00 uplift. This is a structure worth understanding in detail, since it's an unusual sequencing choice most retail-facing M&A commentary glosses over.
  • Granting Brookfield due diligence access in February 2025, after two bidders had already emerged, was a deliberate choice to maximise competitive tension rather than move quickly to a binding deal with the two most advanced parties — a trade-off between speed/certainty and price maximisation.
  • Once Bain withdrew citing macro uncertainty, the board's decision to proceed with CC Capital at $4.80 rather than push harder or accept execution risk by waiting for market conditions to improve reflects a preference for certainty once competitive tension had genuinely broken down — a defensible but not risk-free call, given the independent expert still had to separately confirm fairness.
  • The MAC (material adverse change) clause tied to a forward-looking reference EBITDA, rather than a historic figure, as confirmed by CFO David Chalmers on the FY25 earnings call, meant Insignia's near-term earnings trajectory mattered directly to deal certainty, not just to the headline valuation.

docs.title: 5. What This Demonstrates
docs.text: This case study was built to demonstrate the mechanics that sit behind a Financial Sponsors or M&A analyst's day-to-day work: reconstructing a multi-party competitive process from public disclosures, building a consistent valuation framework across bid stages, and forming a view on the judgment calls a board and its advisers actually had to make, rather than only reading the headline outcome. The accompanying Excel model contains the full deal timeline, financial summary and valuation build with source citations and editable assumptions.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Perpetual Limited, one of Australia's oldest financial services groups (Asset Management, Corporate Trust, and until recently Wealth Management), has been the subject of three successive non-binding takeover proposals from EQT AB since 1 July 2026, rising from $21.64 to $22.07 to $22.50 per share. The Perpetual board has rejected all three, most recently on 28-29 July 2026, but has now granted EQT limited, non-exclusive access to non-public information to help formulate an improved offer. As of the most recent traded price, the stock sits meaningfully below the latest rejected bid, suggesting the market is not yet pricing in a high probability of a higher offer or deal completion.

The situation is complicated by a second, related transaction: Perpetual has separately agreed to sell its Wealth Management division to Bain Capital for $500 million upfront plus up to $100 million in contingent earnout, targeted to complete in Q4 CY2026. Completion of that sale is itself a stated condition of any binding EQT transaction, meaning two deals now need to land in sequence before shareholders see a resolution. This is not Perpetual's first encounter with private equity: a Scheme Implementation Deed with KKR, covering Wealth Management and Corporate Trust, was terminated in February 2025 after Perpetual had already begun operationally separating its divisions in preparation for it.

docs.title: 1. Company Overview
docs.text:
Perpetual (ASX: PPT), founded in 1886, operates two remaining core divisions following the Wealth Management divestment: Asset Management, a global multi-boutique manager spanning equities, credit, fixed income and multi-asset strategies (including boutiques such as J O Hambro, Barrow Hanley and TSW) with $219.2 billion in AUM as at 31 December 2025; and Corporate Trust, a fiduciary and digital services business spanning Debt Market Services, Managed Funds Services, and Digital and Markets, administering roughly $1.3 trillion in funds under administration.

Metric FY24 FY25 1H26 (to Dec-25) Revenue ($m) 1,360 1,373.0 697.9 UPAT ($m) 206.1 204.1 n/a (UPAT +12% YoY reported) Statutory NPAT ($m) (472.2) (58.2) 53.9 Asset Mgmt AUM ($bn, period-end) n/a 226.8 219.2

FY25's large statutory loss reflects a $134.6 million impairment, predominantly relating to the J O Hambro boutique, alongside costs tied to the (ultimately terminated) KKR transaction and the ongoing Simplification Program. UPAT — Perpetual's preferred underlying measure — has been comparatively stable, down only 1% in FY25 and up 12% in 1H26, driven by cost discipline more than revenue growth. Asset Management continues to see net outflows even as AUM rises on market performance, a dynamic worth understanding for any valuation view: flows, not just markets, drive the medium-term revenue base a buyer is underwriting.

docs.title: 2. The Bidding Situation
docs.text:
Background — the KKR Scheme (2024-25)

  • Through 2024, Perpetual operationally separated its three divisions in preparation for a Scheme of Arrangement under which KKR would acquire Wealth Management and Corporate Trust, leaving Asset Management as a standalone listed entity.
  • That Scheme Implementation Deed was terminated in February 2025. Perpetual has not disclosed the specific reason in the sources reviewed for this case study, but continued the separation work regardless, since it now supports the current, differently-structured operating model.

Current Situation — EQT AB (July 2026 onward)

  • 1 July 2026: Perpetual entered a trading halt following market reports of an assembled EQT bid; shares surged on the news. EQT's initial proposal, via an entity called Windflower Pte Limited, came in at $21.64 per share — a premium of almost 40% to the undisturbed price — and was rejected the same day as highly conditional and inadequate.
  • 15/17 July 2026: EQT revised to $22.07 per share, a 2% increase; rejected.
  • 26 July 2026: EQT revised further to $22.50 per share, another 2% increase (4% above the original proposal); the board again concluded this was not in shareholders' best interests, but for the first time agreed to grant EQT limited, non-exclusive, confidential access to non-public information to help formulate an improved offer.
  • Completion of the separate Bain Capital Wealth Management sale is a disclosed condition of any binding EQT transaction — meaning EQT's economics are effectively underwriting the post-divestment Asset Management and Corporate Trust stub, not the group as it stands today.

Parallel Transaction — Bain Capital / Wealth Management

  • Perpetual has agreed to sell its Wealth Management division to Bain Capital Private Equity for $500 million upfront cash plus up to $100 million in contingent performance-based earnout, targeting completion in Q4 CY2026 subject to regulatory and court approvals.
  • Management has guided to a pro-forma net debt/EBITDA of approximately 0.2x following completion, reflecting both the sale proceeds and continued gross debt paydown under the Simplification Program.

docs.title: 3. Valuation — The Bid Walk
docs.text:
Applying a consistent share-count basis (112.9m diluted shares, per FY25 disclosure) across each proposal, and a recent aggregator-sourced net debt figure (full detail and formulas in the accompanying Excel model):

Stage Price/Share Equity Value EV EV/TTM EBITDA Premium to Undisturbed Pre-approach (~29-Jun-26) $15.50 $1,750m $2,333m 6.4x - EQT initial (1-Jul-26) $21.64 $2,443m $3,026m 8.3x 39.6% EQT revised (15/17-Jul-26) $22.07 $2,491m $3,075m 8.5x 42.4% EQT further revised (26-Jul-26) $22.50 $2,540m $3,123m 8.6x 45.2% Most recent traded price (27-Jul-26) $19.50 $2,201m $2,785m 7.7x 25.8%

The 39.6% premium implied by the initial $21.64 proposal matches press reporting of "almost 40%" closely, a useful sense-check on the assumptions used. The more revealing figure is the gap between the latest rejected bid ($22.50) and the most recent traded price ($19.50): a $3.00, or roughly 13%, discount. In an unresolved bid situation, this gap is effectively the market's own probability-weighted estimate of deal completion risk — a meaningful discount signals the market sees real chance of the process stalling, a lower final price, or a long, uncertain path (consistent with EQT's access being limited and non-exclusive rather than a full exclusivity arrangement).

docs.title: 4. Key Judgment Calls (Advisory Perspective)
docs.text:
Several elements of this situation are genuinely live judgment calls rather than settled facts, which is exactly what makes it a useful one to track in real time:

  • Sequencing two linked transactions (Wealth Management sale to Bain, then a potential EQT deal for the remainder) creates real completion risk and negotiating complexity — EQT is effectively conditioning its offer on a transaction Perpetual doesn't fully control the timing of, since it also needs regulatory and court approval.
  • Granting limited, non-exclusive due diligence access after three rejections, rather than either accepting a bid or shutting the process down, is a deliberate middle path: it keeps optionality open without granting EQT the negotiating leverage that full exclusivity would confer.
  • The board's repeated rejections despite each bid being a premium to the undisturbed price reflect a view that intrinsic value (post-Wealth Management sale, at reduced leverage, potentially benefiting from re-rating as a cleaner Asset Management/Corporate Trust story) exceeds what's currently on the table — a bet worth stress-testing against the AUM outflow trend in Asset Management.
  • The upcoming FY26 results (27 August 2026) will be a genuine inflection point for this analysis — updated guidance, confirmed leverage post-Wealth Management sale, and any commentary on the EQT process will materially move the picture and should prompt an update to this model.

docs.title: 5. What This Demonstrates
docs.text: Unlike a completed transaction, this case study is designed to be tracked and updated in real time — refreshing the valuation table as new proposals or rejections are announced, and revisiting the leverage math once the Wealth Management sale completes. That live-tracking discipline, reading each ASX announcement, updating the model same-day, and forming a fresh view on what the market's reaction implies, is closer to what a Financial Sponsors or M&A analyst actually does day to day than a backward-looking case study alone can demonstrate.

docs.title: Treasuries Rally on Softer Momentum; Gold Surges While Oil Retreats
docs.text:

docs.title: Branch strategy
docs.text:
Trunk-based development with short-lived branches.

  • main is always green and always deployable.
  • One branch per logical unit of work, living no longer than a few days.
  • Branches are never committed to directly. Every change goes through a pull request, gated by CI, and squash-merged.
  • Branch names follow type/short-description, e.g. feat/fred-connector, fix/rba-csv-parsing, docs/adr-0002-duckdb.

docs.title: Commit convention
docs.text:
Conventional Commits: type(scope): imperative summary.

Types: feat, fix, docs, test, refactor, chore, perf, ci.

Commit bodies explain why a change was made, never what changed — the diff already shows what changed.

docs.title: Pull request process
docs.text:
• Every PR is gated by the ci status check (lint, types, tests).
  • Branch protection blocks merging until ci passes.
  • Squash merge only. The squashed commit title becomes the permanent entry in main's history, so it should read well on its own.
  • Head branches are deleted automatically after merge.

docs.title: The rule of three
docs.text: core/ starts empty. A module is extracted into core/ only once three separate applications demonstrate the same concrete requirement. Until then, duplication between apps/ directories is accepted deliberately. Abstractions designed before their third real use are usually wrong.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
• ruff decides all formatting and linting. Do not hand-format code that disagrees with it.
  • Type hints on every function signature. mypy --strict applies to core/ and apps/.
  • Functions stay under roughly 50 lines; modules under roughly 300.
  • Pydantic models sit at every layer boundary. Plain dicts are fine inside a single function, never across a boundary.
  • No bare except:. Catch specific exceptions with context.
  • No print() in library code — use logging.

docs.title: Project reviews
docs.text: Once a month, review the roadmap against reality: what shipped, what's stale, what should be deleted. Deleting a project is a legitimate outcome and should be expected occasionally.

docs.title: The invariant
docs.text:
Language models never produce numbers in this repository.

Every figure that appears in published output — a percentage change, a spread, a rate, a multiple — is computed in Python from data that has been fetched, stored, and validated. The model's role is strictly to narrate figures it is given. It may not calculate, estimate, infer, interpolate, or restate a number that was not present in its input.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text: A single hallucinated figure in a published financial note is enough to destroy the credibility of the entire project. Enforcing this as a written rule, rather than trusting a prompt to hold, is the difference between a demo and a system.

docs.title: How it is enforced
docs.text:
This is a mechanical enforcement, not a prompting convention:

  1. Every LLM call takes a Pydantic-validated payload of already-computed values as its only input.
  2. Every LLM call declares a Pydantic response model whose fields are prose only — headlines, summaries, bullet points. No numeric fields.
  3. Every generated narrative passes a numeric fidelity check before publication: every numeral appearing in the output text must be traceable back to the input payload, within a stated rounding tolerance. If any numeral cannot be traced, the run does not publish. It fails loudly instead.
  4. Temperature is set to 0 for any call whose output will be treated as factual.

docs.title: What this rules out
docs.text:
• Asking a model to "calculate the change" or "work out the spread."
  • Asking a model to summarise a table by restating its numbers from memory rather than being handed the table as structured input.
  • Any prompt whose correctness depends on the model's arithmetic being reliable. It is not assumed to be, regardless of how well it performs in casual testing.

When in doubt: if a task involves a number, write a Python function.

docs.title: What gets a unit test
docs.text: Every function in a calculations/ module has a unit test with a hand-computed expected value. If the expected value was derived by running the code itself, the test proves nothing.

docs.title: What gets a cassette
docs.text:
Any test that would otherwise make a real network call is either:

  • marked @pytest.mark.network and excluded from CI, or
  • backed by a recorded fixture/cassette, so the test is deterministic and does not depend on a third-party API being reachable.

CI never depends on an external service being up. This is enforced by running pytest -m "not network" in the ci workflow.

docs.title: What gets an eval
docs.text: Generative features (anything that calls an LLM) are not considered tested by a unit test alone. They require an eval: a small, hand-labelled dataset with a scoring function, run and reported on explicitly, not just checked for "did it not crash."

docs.title: Coverage targets
docs.text:
• core/: 90% once populated.
  • calculations/ modules specifically: 90%, since these carry the numbers that end up in published output.
  • apps/ generally: no fixed target — coverage on glue code and I/O is less meaningful than coverage on pure logic.

docs.title: The rule that is never broken
docs.text: A failing test is never weakened or deleted to make CI pass. If a test fails, either the code is wrong or the test's expectation was wrong — and if it's the latter, that's stated explicitly in the commit message, not silently patched away.
